LH-REG-002.question: An insurer incorporated in Bermuda wants to sell life insurance policies to residents of Texas. In Texas, this company is classified as:
LH-REG-002.explanation: The Texas Insurance Code defines an alien insurer as one organized under the laws of a foreign country. A foreign insurer is one incorporated in a different U.S. state, which is the tempting choice but applies only to companies formed within the United States.

LH-PROV-004.explanation: Texas requires every life policy to give a grace period of at least one month for each premium after the first, and the policy stays in force during it. Because death occurred within the grace period, the insurer pays the face amount minus the overdue premium: $100,000 - $1,200 = $98,800, not the full $100,000.

LH-PROV-005.explanation: Texas rules let a lapsed policy with nonforfeiture values be reinstated within three years of default, or longer at the insurer's option, on evidence of insurability and payment of overdue premiums with interest. Paying only the missed premium is not enough, and a policy surrendered for cash cannot be reinstated.

LH-HPRV-001.explanation: Texas requires a grace period of at least 10 days for monthly premiums, so coverage continues through June 11 and any unpaid premium can be deducted from a claim. The 7-day minimum applies only to weekly premiums, and 31 days applies to other modes.

LH-GEN-017.explanation: Estoppel prevents a party from reasserting a right after its own conduct led the other party to rely on it giving that right up. By accepting late premiums for two years, the insurer led the owner to rely on that practice, so a court bars the lapse. Indemnity is the principle of restoring an insured to the pre-loss condition and has nothing to do with this dispute.

LH-LIFE-001.question: Maria bought and owns a policy on her husband's life and named herself beneficiary. In their divorce the decree awards her the policy. He dies five years later. The insurer will:
LH-LIFE-001.explanation: For life insurance, insurable interest must exist only when the policy is applied for, not at the time of death, so the divorce does not void Maria's policy. Texas's divorce rule (Family Code 9.301) cancels a spouse designation made by the insured; here Maria owns the policy, made the designation herself and was awarded the policy in the decree.

LH-HPRV-017.explanation: COBRA lets the employer charge up to 102% of the full premium, and 1.02 x $600 = $612. Rita has 60 days to elect, and COBRA lasts up to 18 months after a layoff; for an insured Texas plan, state law then adds up to 6 more months of continuation.

LH-HPRV-016.explanation: COBRA applies to employers with 20 or more employees and allows 36 months for divorce, death of the employee, Medicare entitlement or loss of dependent status. The 18-month period applies to termination or reduced hours, extended to 29 months for a disabled beneficiary. Texas law also lets a divorced spouse continue insured group coverage for up to 3 years.

LH-HLTH-019.explanation: Workers' compensation is no-fault and, for an employer that carries it, the exclusive remedy for work injuries, so the employee gives up the right to sue that employer. Texas employers may choose not to carry it, and those nonsubscribers can be sued. Individual health policies commonly exclude occupational injuries covered by workers' compensation.
